text:
sara.k: Quick RFC follow-up — we need a concrete migration path for service actors to ephemeral tokens. Current constraints: lots of long-lived API keys used by on‑prem agents, CI runners, and a couple of partner integrations. Proposal sketch: short-lived JWTs (5m–1h) via a token-exchange endpoint, legacy-key proxy for fallback, and optional mTLS for high-security tenants. Thoughts? :thinking:

hemant: +1 on short-lived. couple practical concerns: 1) CI workflows that run for hours/parallel jobs, 2) on‑prem agents with intermittent connectivity, 3) audit + replay risk if we mis-handle refresh. we should define refresh window and an offline refresh path.

tia: For CI we can support two modes: an ephemeral token per job (recommended), or a job-scoped refresh token stored in vault with limited TTL. The refresh token should be rotate-on-first-use so compromised vault creds are less useful.

kevin: For on‑prem agents, we need graceful offline auth. Idea: issue a signed long-lived enrollment token at onboarding that can mint ephemeral tokens locally with a TPS-limited local agent process, plus a revocation channel (push via control-plane when agent reconnects). Means we accept one long-lived secret per agent but keep usage ephemeral in practice.

devex-jen: From SDK/CLI perspective: we should expose `redwood auth login --agent` and `redwood auth exchange --subject-token <file>` with built-in refresh + metrics. Also document the recommended CI pattern and provide a GH Action. :+1:

hemant: performance note — token‑exchange adds an extra RTT on hot paths. For low-latency endpoints we should support cached short-lived tokens (client-side) and allow a small leeway in TTL checks (clock skew). Also we can return `recommended_cache_ms` in the exchange response so SDKs know how long to reuse.

sara.k: Good call. We should avoid per-request exchanges. Cache policy example: if TTL=15m, recommend cache 12m, rotate at 80%. We also need to think about quotas: token-exchange traffic could be high for bursty customers.

auth-bot: Security note: require proof-of-possession for token-exchange from agents that can. For webhooks/partners we can allow subject_token types limited by audience. Also log token-exchange events with non-sensitive hashes.

kevin: RBAC mapping question — do ephemeral tokens encode actor identity and project scope, or should exchange return a bound token with claims? I prefer bound tokens (aud=service, scp=project:read) to minimize downstream auth checks.

tia: Bound tokens are better. Encode `actor_id`, `actor_type`, `projects` (list) and `exp`. Keep tokens small; downstream services should only validate signature + exp + audience. Mapping to RBAC can be done at mint time to keep runtime fast.

hemant: For rollout we need a compatibility layer: 1) detect legacy API key in front-door and emit deprecation header `X-RW-Auth-Compat: legacy`; 2) allow legacy keys to call the token-exchange endpoint to get ephemeral tokens (migration bridge); 3) after 6 months disable direct usage of legacy keys but keep exchange for a window and revoke enrollment tokens on demand.

sara.k: Ops + monitoring: define metrics: `token_exchange_count`, `token_exchange_latency_ms`, `legacy_key_direct_calls`, `enrollment_revocations`, `token_issue_errors`. Alerts: spike in `legacy_key_direct_calls` post-deprecation could indicate failed rollout.

devex-jen: Also publish a migration checklist for customers: steps to add SDK, rotate to exchange pattern, update CI, test failover to legacy proxy. Provide sample code:```bash
# exchange pattern (example)
curl -X POST https://auth.redwood.example/v1/token/exchange \n  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \n  -d '{"subject_token":"$ENROLL_TOKEN","requested_tt":"3600"}'
```

kevin: Threat model items: protect enrollment token issuance (human-in-the-loop or limited scope), monitor token-exchange rates per actor (possible worm auth), and ensure revocation path is speedy: revocations should mark caches stale and publish a push event to control-plane so agents refresh immediately.

hemant: Implementation notes: auth service will be stateful for enrollment and revocation; exchange endpoint can be horizontally scaled and stateless (validate enrollment signature + lookup revocation tombstones via a low-latency cache). We'll need a signed mute list with versioning.

sara.k: OK concrete next steps: 1) write an RFC appendix with: token formats, TTLs, exchange API, enrollment flow, revocation semantics, metrics, deprecation timetable (6mo), 2) devex to draft SDK/CLI changes and GH Action, 3) eng to prototype exchange + legacy-proxy, 4) security to finalize proof-of-possession + enrollment gating. Assign owners?

tia: I'll own the SDK/CLI patterns (devex-jen help).

kevin: I'll prototype agent enrollment + local minting flow.

hemant: I'll sketch auth service exchange API and revocation cache design.

devex-jen: I'll draft migration docs & GH Action template.

sara.k: Great. I'll put the RFC appendix into the RFC tracker and schedule a 30m sync next week to lock TTLs and deprecation dates. Thanks all. :rocket:
